title: Palestine: A Beginner's Historical Timeline
subtitle: The main turning points from Ottoman Palestine through the Oslo era, explained carefully and without slogans
summary: Modern Palestine cannot be understood from one date or one war. This short timeline explains the British Mandate, the 1947 partition recommendation, the 1948 Nakba, the occupation that began in 1967, the Intifadas, and the Oslo process. It also shows why Muslims should seek justice without hiding facts that complicate a preferred story.

sections.title: The Story in One Minute
sections.body:
Palestine was part of the Ottoman Empire until the First World War. Britain then governed it under a League of Nations Mandate that supported a Jewish national home while stating that nothing should prejudice the civil and religious rights of the existing non-Jewish communities. Competing national movements, immigration, dispossession, resistance, and violence deepened the conflict.

In 1947 the UN General Assembly recommended partition. War followed, Israel was established, and more than half of the Palestinian Arab population fled or was expelled. Palestinians remember this mass displacement as the Nakba. In 1967 Israel occupied the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and Gaza. Later uprisings and negotiations changed institutions but did not produce a final settlement.

sections.title: Before 1947: Ottoman Rule and the British Mandate
sections.body:
For centuries, the land was governed as part of the Ottoman Empire. Its towns and villages included Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians, long-established Jewish communities, and other groups. Modern Palestinian and Zionist national movements developed during the late Ottoman and Mandate periods.

In the [Balfour Declaration of 1917](https://www.un.org/unispal/document/auto-insert-193242/), Britain supported establishing a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine. The declaration also said that the civil and religious rights of the existing non-Jewish communities should not be prejudiced. The [League of Nations Mandate](https://www.un.org/unispal/document/auto-insert-201057/) incorporated this policy in 1922. Jewish immigration grew, especially as European Jews fled persecution. Palestinian Arabs sought independence and opposed policies they believed threatened their political and national rights. The period included protest, rebellion, communal attacks, and violence by multiple armed actors.

sections.title: 1947-1949: Partition, War, and the Nakba
sections.body:
In November 1947, [UN General Assembly Resolution 181](https://www.un.org/unispal/document/auto-insert-185393/) recommended ending the Mandate and creating an Arab state and a Jewish state, with a special international regime for Jerusalem. It was a General Assembly recommendation, not a negotiated agreement between the communities, and the plan was not implemented as written. Jewish Agency leaders accepted it as a basis for statehood; Palestinian Arab leaders and neighboring Arab governments rejected it.

Fighting began before Britain left. Israel declared independence in May 1948, and neighboring Arab states entered the war. During the conflict, roughly 750,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, with circumstances varying by place. Palestinians call this mass displacement and dispossession the Nakba, Arabic for “catastrophe.” The [United Nations Nakba overview](https://www.un.org/unispal/about-the-nakba/) documents the scale while fuller histories examine local causes and decisions.

sections.title: 1967: Occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza
sections.body:
In the June 1967 war, Israel captured the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip, as well as other Arab territories. [UN Security Council Resolution 242](https://www.un.org/unispal/document/auto-insert-184858/) emphasized that territory cannot lawfully be acquired by war and called for a just and lasting peace, including Israeli withdrawal from territories occupied in the conflict and a just settlement of the refugee problem.

The [International Committee of the Red Cross](https://www.icrc.org/en/document/ihl-occupying-power-responsibilities-occupied-palestinian-territories) treats the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza as occupied territory. The [International Court of Justice held in 2024](https://www.icj-cij.org/node/204176) that Israel's withdrawal from Gaza did not entirely release it from occupation-law obligations; those obligations remain commensurate with its effective control. Israel disputes the post-2005 characterization of Gaza. The legal disagreement should be stated, but it does not remove the protections that international humanitarian law gives civilians.

sections.title: 1987-2000s: Uprisings and the Oslo Process
sections.body:
The [First Intifada began in 1987](https://www.un.org/unispal/history/) as a Palestinian uprising against occupation. It included strikes, boycotts, demonstrations, civil disobedience, stone-throwing, and armed violence. Israeli responses included military and policing measures. Civilians suffered.

In 1993, Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization signed the [Oslo Declaration of Principles](https://peacemaker.un.org/en/node/9432). It created a framework for limited Palestinian self-government during an interim period and left Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, security, and borders for later talks. It did not end the occupation or create a sovereign Palestinian state.

The [Second Intifada erupted in September 2000](https://www.un.org/unispal/history/) amid rising tensions and failed final-status talks. Its causes should not be reduced to one meeting or event. It included attacks on Israeli civilians, armed clashes, Israeli military operations, and severe harm to Palestinian civilians. A truthful account does not excuse attacks on civilians by any side.

sections.title: How a Muslim Should Read This History
sections.body:
A timeline is a starting point, not a complete moral verdict. Each period contains disputed motives, local differences, and human stories that a short article cannot settle. Read primary documents, note who produced each source, and distinguish a legal finding from a political claim or personal memory.

Quran 5:8 gives Muslims a demanding rule: hatred must not push a believer away from justice. That means refusing denial of Palestinian dispossession, refusing hatred of Jews as a people, and refusing excuses for attacks on civilians. Supporting Palestinian freedom and dignity is strongest when it is joined to accuracy, mercy, and accountability before Allah.

sections.title: Key Takeaways: Palestine's Modern Timeline
sections.body: The conflict grew through the Mandate, competing national projects, the 1948 war and Nakba, occupation after 1967, uprisings, and incomplete negotiations. No single date explains everything. A fair reading keeps Palestinian displacement and rights at the center while recognizing the safety and dignity of every civilian.

quranVerses.translation: O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.

furtherReading.title: History of the Question of Palestine
furtherReading.author: United Nations
furtherReading.note: A continuously maintained institutional overview of the Mandate, partition, 1948, 1967, and later UN involvement; use it as a documented UN chronology, not as the only historical interpretation.

furtherReading.title: Palestine Plan of Partition with Economic Union — Resolution 181 (II)
furtherReading.author: United Nations General Assembly
furtherReading.note: The primary text of the General Assembly's partition recommendation and its proposed arrangements for Jerusalem and the two states.

furtherReading.title: Security Council Resolution 242
furtherReading.author: United Nations Security Council
furtherReading.note: The primary resolution that framed later diplomacy around withdrawal, peace, security, and a just settlement of the refugee problem.

furtherReading.title: Declaration of Principles on Interim Self-Government Arrangements
furtherReading.author: Government of Israel and Palestine Liberation Organization
furtherReading.note: The Oslo Declaration of Principles; it established an interim framework and deferred permanent-status questions.

furtherReading.title: Responsibilities of an Occupying Power in the Occupied Palestinian Territory
furtherReading.author: International Committee of the Red Cross
furtherReading.note: Explains the ICRC's legal position on the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza and the humanitarian protections that flow from occupation law.
